blocks.body:
Pick any $51$ distinct numbers from $1$ to $100$. Must one of them divide another? The answer is yes, and the proof is two lines once you look at the right feature of each number. No theory of primes is needed beyond the fact that every number is a power of $2$ times an odd number.

Combinatorial number theory is the art of such arguments: questions about sets of integers where the decisive step is counting, pigeonholing or an extremal choice rather than algebra. Most of Erdős's famous problems on sums, divisors and progressions are phrased this way. Learning the basic moves is the entry ticket to them.

blocks.title: Three basic moves
blocks.body:
Almost every argument at this level combines three ingredients.

1. Pigeonhole on a cleverly chosen label. Give each integer a label from a small set, such as its residue mod $n$, its odd part, or the parity vector of its prime exponents. If there are more integers than labels, two share a label, and sharing a label must force the conclusion. Choosing the label is the whole problem.
2. Double counting. Count one set of pairs in two ways, for example pairs $(d,n)$ with $d\mid n$ counted by $n$ or by $d$.
3. Extremal bound plus construction. To find the largest set with some property, prove an upper bound and exhibit a set that attains it. Neither half alone is an answer.

We will see each in action, starting with the theorem from the introduction (see [[pigeonhole]] for the general principle).

blocks.title: Divisor pairs in [1, 2n]
blocks.body: Among any $n+1$ distinct integers in $\{1,2,\dots,2n\}$ there are two, one of which divides the other. The number $n+1$ cannot be lowered: the $n$ integers $n+1,n+2,\dots,2n$ contain no such pair.

Write each chosen integer as $2^km$ with $m$ odd (possible and unique by [[fta]]). The odd part $m$ lies in $\{1,3,\dots,2n-1\}$, a set of $n$ values. With $n+1$ integers, two have the same odd part, say $2^km$ and $2^lm$ with $k\lt l$, and then $2^km\mid2^lm$.

For the second claim: if $n+1\le a\lt b\le2n$ and $a\mid b$, then $b\ge2a\ge2n+2$, which is impossible.

blocks.title: Pigeonhole on residues
blocks.body: Let $a_1,\dots,a_n$ be any integers. Show that some block $a_{i+1}+a_{i+2}+\dots+a_j$ with $0\le i\lt j\le n$ is divisible by $n$.
blocks.solution:
Consider the $n+1$ prefix sums $s_0=0$, $s_1=a_1$, $s_2=a_1+a_2$, $\dots$, $s_n=a_1+\dots+a_n$. There are only $n$ residues mod $n$, so two of them agree: $s_i\equiv s_j\pmod n$ with $i\lt j$. Then $s_j-s_i=a_{i+1}+\dots+a_j$ is divisible by $n$.

The bound is sharp: $n-1$ ones have no nonempty sub-sum divisible by $n$. A deeper relative is the Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv theorem (1961): among any $2n-1$ integers some $n$ of them have sum divisible by $n$. That count is also sharp, since $n-1$ zeros and $n-1$ ones admit no such choice. Its proof needs more than pigeonhole, and we omit it.

blocks.title: Exponent vectors
blocks.body: Seventeen positive integers have all their prime factors in $\{2,3,5,7\}$. Show that two of them have a product that is a perfect square. Show that sixteen would not be enough.
blocks.solution:
Write each number as $2^{e_1}3^{e_2}5^{e_3}7^{e_4}$ and label it by the parity vector $(e_1\bmod2,\dots,e_4\bmod2)\in\{0,1\}^4$. There are $2^4=16$ labels, so two of the seventeen numbers share a label. In their product every exponent is even, so the product is a square.

With sixteen numbers this can fail. Take the $16$ squarefree divisors of $210=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7$. Their parity vectors are all different, and the product of two numbers is a square only when their parity vectors agree. So no two distinct ones have a square product.

Linear algebra over $\mathbb F_2$ gives more: among any five such numbers some nonempty subset has a square product, because five vectors in $\mathbb F_2^4$ are linearly dependent (see [[linear-algebra]]).

blocks.title: Double counting divisors
blocks.body:
How many divisors does an integer up to $n$ have on average? Count the pairs $(d,k)$ with $d\mid k$ and $1\le k\le n$. Grouping by $k$ gives $\sum_{k\le n}\tau(k)$. Grouping by $d$, the multiples of $d$ up to $n$ number $\lfloor n/d\rfloor$. So
$$\sum_{k=1}^{n}\tau(k)=\sum_{d=1}^{n}\Bigl\lfloor\frac nd\Bigr\rfloor.$$
For $n=10$ both sides equal $27$: on the left $1+2+2+3+2+4+2+4+3+4$, on the right $10+5+3+2+2+1+1+1+1+1$. Since $\lfloor n/d\rfloor$ differs from $n/d$ by less than $1$, the right side is $n\sum_{d\le n}1/d+O(n)=n\log n+O(n)$. So an integer up to $n$ has about $\log n$ divisors on average, even though $\tau$ itself jumps around wildly.

blocks.title: Largest sum-free subset of [1, n]
blocks.body: A set $A$ of integers is sum-free if there are no $x,y,z\in A$ (not necessarily distinct) with $x+y=z$. The largest sum-free subset of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ has exactly $\lceil n/2\rceil$ elements.

Construction: the odd numbers in $[1,n]$ form a sum-free set (odd plus odd is even), and there are $\lceil n/2\rceil$ of them.

Upper bound: let $A\subseteq[1,n]$ be sum-free and nonempty, with largest element $a$. Put $B=A\setminus\{a\}$ and $C=\{a-x:x\in B\}$. Both are subsets of $[1,a-1]$ with $|B|=|C|=|A|-1$. They are disjoint: if $a-x\in A$ for some $x\in B$, then $x+(a-x)=a$ is a forbidden sum (this includes the case $x=a-x$). Hence $2(|A|-1)\le a-1\le n-1$, so $|A|\le(n+1)/2$, that is, $|A|\le\lceil n/2\rceil$.

blocks.title: No element twice another
blocks.body: What is the largest subset of $\{1,2,\dots,100\}$ containing no two elements with one equal to twice the other?
blocks.solution:
Group the numbers into chains by odd part: for odd $m\le100$ let $C_m=\{m,2m,4m,\dots\}\cap[1,100]$. If $y=2x$ then $x$ and $y$ have the same odd part, so forbidden pairs only occur inside a chain, and there they are exactly consecutive members. A chain of length $L$ is a path $m-2m-4m-\cdots$. A set containing no two consecutive members has at most $\lceil L/2\rceil$ of them, and taking every other one, starting with the first, attains that. So the answer is $\sum_m\lceil L_m/2\rceil$.

The chain lengths:

- $m=1$: $1,2,\dots,64$, so $L=7$, contributing $4$.
- $m=3$: $3,\dots,96$, so $L=6$, contributing $3$.
- $m=5$: $5,\dots,80$, so $L=5$, contributing $3$.
- $m=7,9,11$: $L=4$, contributing $2$ each, total $6$.
- Odd $m$ from $13$ to $25$ (seven values): $L=3$, contributing $2$ each, total $14$.
- Odd $m$ from $27$ to $49$ (twelve values): $L=2$, contributing $1$ each, total $12$.
- Odd $m$ from $51$ to $99$ (twenty-five values): $L=1$, contributing $25$.

Total: $4+3+3+6+14+12+25=67$. The upper bound and the construction both come from the chain decomposition. That is typical: once the right partition is found, the extremal problem splits into tiny independent problems.

blocks.body:
- Distinctness matters. If repeats were allowed, choosing the same number twice would make "one divides another" trivial; the theorem is about $n+1$ distinct numbers.
- Count the boxes carefully. In the prefix-sum argument there are $n+1$ prefix sums, including the empty sum $s_0=0$. Forgetting $s_0$ loses the argument.
- An upper bound is not an answer until a construction matches it, and a construction is not an answer until it is proved optimal.
- Maximal is not maximum. In $[1,6]$ the set $\{2,3\}$ is sum-free and cannot be enlarged (adding $1,4,5,6$ creates $1+1=2$, $2+2=4$, $2+3=5$, $3+3=6$), yet $\{1,3,5\}$ is larger. A greedy construction that stops when stuck proves nothing about the maximum.

Each of the moves above grows into a field. Sets with no element dividing another are [[primitive-sets]], where Erdős proved that $\sum1/(a\log a)$ stays bounded. Sum-free sets and their colouring versions lead to Schur's theorem in [[ramsey-arithmetic]]. Sizes of sumsets $A+B$ are the subject of [[additive-combinatorics]], and sets with all pairwise sums distinct are [[sidon-sets]]. Representing $1$ as a sum of distinct unit fractions is [[unit-fractions]], and covering all integers by residue classes with distinct moduli is [[covering-systems]]. The exponent-vector trick is the first step of factoring algorithms such as the quadratic sieve, and its linear-algebra form is part of [[linear-algebra]]. Behind all of this sit [[divisibility]], [[fta]] and [[pigeonhole]].

1. Prove that every positive integer $n$ has a nonzero multiple whose decimal digits are all $0$ or $1$.
2. Show that among any $n+1$ integers from $\{1,\dots,2n\}$ two are coprime. Is $n+1$ best possible?
3. Show that among any $k+1$ positive integers whose prime factors all lie in a fixed set of $k$ primes, some nonempty subset has a perfect-square product.
4. Find the largest subset of $\{1,\dots,50\}$ in which no element is three times another.
